opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's one of those things that sounds trivial until you actually try to do it at scale. On paper, a protein structure is just a list of atoms with coordinates, so you'd think you could read the file and move on. In practice, the data in the Protein Data Bank has accumulated over fifty years, from many different labs, experimental methods, and file format conventions, and all of that history shows up in the files.

You have the legacy PDB format, which has fixed-width columns and hard limits on things like the number of atoms or chain identifiers. Then you have mmCIF, which is much more expressive but also much more complicated, and different tools interpret it in slightly different ways. On top of that you get alternate conformations, where an atom might be in two places with partial occupancy. You get missing residues and missing side chains because the density wasn't resolved. You get modified residues, ligands, waters, and ions mixed in with the chains. You get multiple models from NMR, and the asymmetric unit versus the biological assembly from crystallography. Sometimes the sequence in the header doesn't match the coordinates that were actually observed.

Every one of those cases forces a decision, and if you're training a model, those decisions quietly become part of your data distribution. If you drop alternate locations one way, or handle missing residues a certain way, or build the biological assembly differently, you can end up with subtly different training sets. Then your model's behavior changes and it's really hard to trace why.

So the difficulty isn't one hard algorithm. It's thousands of edge cases, and you need to handle all of them consistently, correctly, and fast enough to process the whole PDB, ideally many times as you iterate. Most existing tools were built for a structural biologist looking at one structure at a time, not for an ML pipeline pulling millions of examples. Bridging that gap is a real engineering problem, and it's undervalued because it isn't glamorous. But if your parsing is wrong, nothing downstream can fix it.

r001.rationale: The response says alternate conformations can place an atom in two locations with partial occupancy, communicating alternative positions and positional uncertainty.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so people are always surprised by this. They assume a protein structure is just a list of atoms with coordinates, you read it in, you're done. And in principle that's true. In practice, the data lives in these legacy formats, PDB and mmCIF, that have accumulated decades of edge cases, and almost every one of them bites you eventually.

So take something simple like residue numbering. You'd think residues go one, two, three, four. But the PDB allows insertion codes, so you can have residue 52, 52A, 52B, 52C, because somebody numbered their antibody according to a reference scheme from the seventies. You can have negative residue numbers. You can have gaps where the crystallographer couldn't resolve a loop, so residues 100 through 110 just aren't there. And whether your model should see that as "there's a gap" or "these are consecutive" is actually a modeling decision you have to make explicitly.

Then there's alternate locations. A single atom can have two or three sets of coordinates with occupancies because the side chain is flipping between conformations in the crystal. Most people just take the first one and move on, but you have to actually handle it or your atom counts come out wrong and downstream everything breaks silently.

And then the stuff that's not protein. Waters, ligands, ions, modified residues like selenomethionine that are chemically a standard amino acid but have a different three-letter code. Glycans hanging off asparagines. If you're training a model, you have to decide for every one of these: is this part of the input, is it noise, is it a target. And the files don't tell you, they just dump it all in the same table.

Multiple chains and biological assemblies are another one. The asymmetric unit in a crystal is not necessarily the biological molecule. Sometimes you need to apply symmetry operations to reconstruct the actual complex, and that information is in a separate block of the file with its own conventions.

So what ends up happening is everybody writes their own parser, and everybody's parser is subtly wrong in different ways, and those bugs propagate into training sets and you don't find out until you're six weeks into a run and the model is doing something weird on antibodies specifically. I've honestly spent more time on data loading and cleaning than on model architecture in a lot of projects, and I think that's true for most people doing this seriously, they just don't talk about it because it's not glamorous.

r001.rationale: It says a single atom can have multiple coordinate sets with occupancies because a side chain may occupy different conformations, describing alternative positions for the same part.

astra-6.text:
Because there’s a big gap between reading a structure file and turning it into something you can reliably use. You might think, “It’s just a list of atoms and coordinates.” But then you have to ask: Which atoms are missing? Are there multiple conformations? How do the residues in the structure map back to the protein sequence? What do you do with modified residues or molecules that aren’t proteins?

And those decisions matter downstream. A parser can successfully read a file and still give you a misleading representation of the biology. So the hard part is handling all those cases consistently, while preserving enough information that you’re not silently making assumptions that break your analysis or your model.

r001.rationale: The response asks whether a structure has multiple conformations, but does not state that the data encode uncertainty by giving alternative positions for the same part.

sol-6.1.text:
There’s a big gap between reading a structure file and turning it into something you can reliably use in a model. You might expect a clean list of atoms and coordinates, but you encounter missing residues, alternate conformations, multiple chains, and numbering that doesn’t line up neatly with the sequence. Then you have to decide what each of those things means for your application.

The hard part is that a parser can run successfully and still give you the wrong biological interpretation. Which chains belong together? Is a missing atom something you can reconstruct, or should you exclude that example? Those decisions affect everything downstream. So it’s not just a file-format problem. It’s an engineering problem where you need enough biological understanding to know when your software is silently making a bad assumption.

r001.rationale: The response mentions “alternate conformations,” but does not explain that these encode positional uncertainty by giving multiple positions for the same part.
